subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: In the Class 4 lunch hall of the school in Darjeeling, the girls had a rule this week: nobody sits with Rinku. Dolma didn't start it. But when Rinku came towards their bench with her tiffin, Dolma moved her bag onto the empty space, like everyone else. Rinku stood there, then went and sat on the steps alone. Anirban sir had seen it from the corridor. After lunch he called Dolma to the staff room. 'Why did you put your bag there?' Dolma twisted her plait. 'Everyone was doing it, sir. It wasn't just me.' 'How many bags were on the bench?' 'Six.' 'And whose bag was on Rinku's place?' Dolma looked at her shoes. 'Mine.' 'So one of the six was you.' Her eyes filled. 'Tomorrow,' Anirban sir said, 'you can choose again.'

qa.q: How many bags were on the bench?
qa.a: There were six bags on the bench.

qa.q: Why did 'Everyone was doing it' make Dolma feel less responsible?
qa.a: When six children did the same thing, Dolma's part felt small and shared, as if no one person had really chosen to leave Rinku out.

qa.q: Which question from Anirban sir helped most, and why?
qa.a: 'Whose bag was on Rinku's place?' pointed Dolma to her own choice, so she could see that one of the six was her, not just 'everyone'.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Rinku?
qa.a: Rinku stood with her tiffin, found the bench blocked, and sat alone on the steps, likely feeling hurt and unwanted.

grounding: Shows a child who joins classmates in shutting a girl out at lunch and says everyone was doing it, until a teacher helps her see her own part.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: I'm Eshaan, Chinmay's older brother. Last Sunday I was on the balcony when the building kids picked cricket teams in the compound. Ravi from the second floor, the new boy, stood waiting. One of the big boys said, 'Not him,' and everyone turned their backs. Chinmay turned his back too. Ravi went upstairs. At dinner I asked Chinmay about it. He shrugged. 'Everyone did it. It wasn't my idea.' I said, 'But you did it too.' He said, 'If I didn't, they'd leave me out.' I don't know everything he felt. He didn't finish his rice. The next evening I saw Chinmay knock on the second-floor door with his bat. I don't know what he said. But Ravi came down with him.

qa.q: Who said 'Not him' about Ravi?
qa.a: One of the big boys said, 'Not him.'

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been worried about when he turned his back?
qa.a: Chinmay seemed worried that if he didn't go along, the group would leave him out too, so following everyone felt safer.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make the next evening, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Chinmay knocked on Ravi's door with his bat and brought him down, which showed he could make his own choice instead of hiding inside the group's.

qa.q: What was it like for Ravi, the new boy, when everyone turned their backs?
qa.a: Ravi was likely hurt and embarrassed, standing alone in a new building before going upstairs without a game.

grounding: Shows, through an older brother's eyes, a child who joins the group in shutting out a new boy and says everyone did it, then later makes his own choice.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Monday: At the science project table, the group decided Gurleen would not be in it. 'She's too slow,' someone said. Kishore didn't say anything. He just didn't pass her the chart paper when she reached for it.
Tuesday: Gurleen worked alone at the back. Ma'am asked Kishore's group why she wasn't with them. Kishore said, 'Everyone decided, Ma'am. Not me.' Ma'am asked, 'Did you pass her the chart paper?' Kishore went hot. 'No.'
Thursday: Kishore couldn't stop thinking about the chart paper. It had been in his hands, not everyone's. At the start of the period he carried a roll of it to Gurleen's desk. 'Our group needs someone to draw the diagram. You're good at diagrams.' Gurleen looked up, surprised, and took it.

qa.q: What did Kishore not pass to Gurleen on Monday?
qa.a: Kishore didn't pass her the chart paper.

qa.q: What was Kishore thinking about by Thursday?
qa.a: Kishore felt guilty, realising the chart paper had been in his own hands, so leaving Gurleen out wasn't only 'everyone's' doing.

qa.q: What was the turning point that led Kishore to act?
qa.a: Ma'am's question 'Did you pass her the chart paper?' made Kishore see his own action, and by Thursday he chose to invite Gurleen back to draw the diagram.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt working alone at the back on Tuesday?
qa.a: Gurleen likely felt left out and hurt, shut out of a group without anyone telling her why to her face.

grounding: Shows a child who helps exclude a classmate and says 'everyone decided', until a teacher's question helps him see and repair his own part.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Ojas, you said everyone in your class ignored the new boy, so it wasn't really you. Let me tell you about Bhola.
In Class 5 in Jabalpur, Bhola's father sold milk, and his shirt smelled of the cowshed. One morning a boy in the assembly line held his nose, and soon the whole line did. I held mine too. It felt like a game. For weeks nobody walked to school with Bhola.
When my Amma found out, I said, 'Everyone was doing it!'
She asked, 'Then how much of it was yours, Harish?'
I said, 'Only a little.'
'And Bhola,' she said, 'did he get only a little hurt?'
The next day I walked beside him. Two other boys followed.
So, Ojas, what part of today was yours?

qa.q: What did the boys in the assembly line do to Bhola that morning?
qa.a: One boy held his nose at Bhola, and soon the whole line did, Harish included.

qa.q: Why did holding the nose feel acceptable to young Harish at the time?
qa.a: Because the whole line was doing it, it felt like a game and only 'a little' Harish's fault; being one of many made the act feel shared and small.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Harish, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Amma's question, whether Bhola got 'only a little hurt', was the turning point; the next day Harish chose to walk beside Bhola, and two other boys followed.

qa.q: How might Bhola have experienced those weeks, compared with how the boys saw them?
qa.a: To the boys it was a shared game with each doing only a little, but Bhola walked to school alone every day and carried the whole weight of it.

grounding: An elder recalls joining a whole line in shunning a classmate and claiming everyone was doing it, showing how a shared act feels like no one's fault.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof, so Class 6B was stuck inside for recess. Nikhita drew a chalk square on the floor: 'Secret club. Members only.' Eight girls squeezed in. When Mehak came over with her ludo board, Nikhita said, 'Full.' Then she looked at Disha. 'Right, Disha?'
Disha glanced at the others. Everyone was nodding. 'Full,' she repeated.
Mehak sat alone by the dripping window, lining up ludo pieces nobody would move.
Later, Ms Rao asked the club what had happened. 'I only said one word,' Disha said. 'Everyone else said it first.'
'Eight people, one word each,' Ms Rao said. 'How many words did Mehak hear?'
Disha counted on her fingers and stopped at eight. She looked over at the window.

qa.q: What did Mehak bring over to the chalk square?
qa.a: Mehak came over with her ludo board.

qa.q: Why did saying 'Full' feel small to Disha?
qa.a: Disha felt it was only one word and everyone else had said it first, so the blame seemed spread across the whole group rather than resting on her.

qa.q: When Disha looks over at the window, what choice could she make next?
qa.a: Disha could go and play ludo with Mehak or tell the club there is room; one person stepping out of the group can start to undo those eight words.

qa.q: What was recess like for Mehak by the dripping window?
qa.a: Mehak heard 'Full' from the whole group and spent recess alone lining up pieces; to her it felt like being turned away eight times, not once. 😔

grounding: A child who joins a group in shutting a classmate out says everyone else said it first, as if the shared act belonged to no one.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: At recess in the government school at Meenangadi, Class 5 played seven-stones under the jackfruit tree. When Thomas ran over, Anitha said, 'No space. Go away.' Everyone laughed and turned their backs, and Reena turned hers too. Thomas stood there for a while, then went and sat on the steps alone. After school, when Reena's Amma asked why she was so quiet, Reena said, 'Thomas cried a little. But it wasn't me. Everyone told him to go. I only did what they did.' Amma put down the rice pot. 'So if twenty people turn their backs, it's nobody's back?' Reena frowned. 'It was mostly Anitha.' 'And whose back was yours?' Reena didn't answer. She was thinking about Thomas on the steps.

qa.q: Where did Class 5 play seven-stones?
qa.a: They played under the jackfruit tree.

qa.q: Why did Reena say 'I only did what they did'?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and a bit guilty about Thomas crying, and sharing the blame with everyone made her part feel smaller.

qa.q: What could Reena do tomorrow?
qa.a: She could invite Thomas to play or sit with him, and say sorry for turning her back, instead of waiting for the others.

qa.q: What was recess like for Thomas?
qa.a: He was hurt and alone, sitting on the steps after everyone turned their backs, and he cried a little.

grounding: A child who joins in turning away a classmate says everyone did it, so her own part feels like no one's.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: In the school canteen in Lisbon, the girls at Beatriz's table had a new rule: Noa couldn't sit with them anymore, because Marta said so. When Noa came over with her tray, everyone spread their bags across the empty chairs. Beatriz put her bag down too. Noa stood there holding the tray, then walked to the table by the bins. At dinner, Beatriz's father asked about her day. 'Noa cried at lunch,' she said, pushing peas around. 'But it's not my fault. Everyone put their bags on the chairs. I was just doing what the others did.' Her father waited. 'How many bags were on the chairs?' 'Five.' 'And whose was the fifth?' Beatriz stared at her peas. 'Mine,' she said, very quietly.

qa.q: Where did Noa go to sit?
qa.a: Noa walked to the table by the bins.

qa.q: Why did Beatriz say it was not her fault?
qa.a: She felt guilty about Noa crying, and since everyone put bags down, spreading the blame across the group made her own part feel less real.

qa.q: How did her father help Beatriz see her part?
qa.a: He asked how many bags there were and whose was the fifth, so she had to name her own action.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Noa?
qa.a: Noa was hurt and humiliated, standing with her tray while bags blocked every chair, and ended up crying at the table by the bins.

grounding: A child who helped block a classmate from the lunch table says everyone did it, until her father asks whose bag was hers.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: At the summer camp run by the community centre, each cabin had to choose teammates for the treasure hunt. The girls from Cabin 3 agreed, in whispers, that nobody would pick Vasudha, because she was 'weird' and talked too much about insects. Zeenat didn't think she was weird. But when the counsellor asked who wanted Vasudha, Zeenat kept her hand down like everyone else. Vasudha was put with the counsellors' team. Later, at the water tank, the counsellor, Mrs Rego, asked Zeenat why nobody had picked her. 'Everyone decided,' Zeenat said. 'I didn't say anything mean. Nobody picked her.' Mrs Rego nodded. 'When everybody does it, each person thinks it was nobody. But it was nine hands staying down. One of them was yours.' Zeenat looked at her wet hands.

qa.q: Which team was Vasudha put with?
qa.a: Vasudha was put with the counsellors' team.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat keep her hand down even though she didn't think Vasudha was weird?
qa.a: She felt nervous about going against the group, and when everyone did the same, her own part seemed not to count.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do at the next activity?
qa.a: She could pick Vasudha or sit with her even if nobody else does, since one person breaking the pattern matters.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel being put with the counsellors' team?
qa.a: Vasudha might feel lonely and embarrassed, noticing that no one her age chose her.

grounding: A child at camp joins the group in not picking a classmate and says everyone decided, until an adult points out her own hand.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Monday: At lunch, Madhuri asked to join the skipping game. Rukmini said, “No space,” and the others turned their backs. Keerthana turned her back too.
Wednesday: Miss Pereira had noticed. She asked Keerthana why Madhuri sat alone at every break. Keerthana looked at her shoes. “Everyone said no, Miss. I didn't start it. I just did what the others did.”
“And if you had said yes?”
Keerthana shrugged. It felt small, being one of eight.
Friday: Madhuri's tiffin fell and her rice spilled on the steps. Nobody moved. Keerthana stood with the rope in her hand and thought, If everyone waits for everyone, nobody ever helps. Her stomach felt tight. She walked over, picked up the tiffin lid and said, “You can take my end of the rope.”

qa.q: What did Keerthana say to Miss Pereira on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said, “Everyone said no, Miss. I didn't start it. I just did what the others did.”

qa.q: Why did it feel reasonable to Keerthana to turn her back on Monday?
qa.a: Being one of eight made her feel less responsible, and she was probably afraid of standing out from the group.

qa.q: What small step helped on Friday, and what could she try next?
qa.a: Walking over and offering her end of the rope; next she could ask Madhuri to join the game from the start of break.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri when the whole group turns away?
qa.a: She is left lonely and exposed, and it doesn't matter to her who started it, because everyone's back feels the same.

grounding: The passage shows a child joining a group exclusion and saying everyone else did it, with responsibility spread thin across the group.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Vidya, come sit. You said Tanvir is being left out and it isn't your doing. Let me, your Nana Wasim, tell you something.
When I was ten, in Mhow, there was a boy called Shafiq who stammered. The rest of us decided he couldn't play gilli-danda with us. I didn't decide it, you see. Iqbal decided it. I just stood with Iqbal.
For a whole summer Shafiq watched from the wall. When my Abbu asked, I said, “All the boys agreed.” I was so sure that made it nobody's fault.
Then Shafiq's family moved away. On the last day he waved at me, only me, because once, long before, I had shared my guava with him.
I still think of that wave. Eight of us kept him out, but I was one whole person in those eight.

qa.q: What game did the boys keep Shafiq out of?
qa.a: They kept him out of gilli-danda for a whole summer.

qa.q: Why did young Wasim feel sure that it was nobody's fault?
qa.a: He felt safe inside the group; because all the boys agreed and Iqbal decided, his own part felt too small to count.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Wasim have made a different choice?
qa.a: When his Abbu asked him; instead of saying “All the boys agreed,” he could have admitted his part and invited Shafiq to play.

qa.q: How might Shafiq have felt, watching from the wall all summer?
qa.a: Lonely and rejected, and the wave on the last day suggests he still hoped someone would be his friend.

grounding: The elder's memory shows a boy joining in excluding a classmate and saying all the boys agreed, so no one felt fully responsible.

passage:
It had rained since morning, so break was inside, all thirty-two of them squeezed into Class 5B with the windows shut and the fan broken.
Someone had drawn a cricket pitch in chalk between the benches. Hemant was batting when Wasim came over with his eraser-ball.
“Can I bowl?”
Farhan said, “Team's full.” The team was not full. Three others said, “Full, full,” and Hemant said it too, loudly, because everyone else was.
Wasim went back to his bench and pretended to read.
Ten minutes later, Sister Agnes asked who had told Wasim he could not play. Nobody answered. Then Hemant said, “Not me alone, Sister. All of us said it.”
Saying it out loud, he felt his ears go hot. All of us had sounded like a good excuse in his head. Out loud it sounded like he had simply joined in.

qa.q: What did Hemant say when Sister Agnes asked who had told Wasim he could not play?
qa.a: He said, “Not me alone, Sister. All of us said it.”

qa.q: Why did Hemant's ears go hot when he spoke?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, because the excuse that sounded fair in his head now sounded like simply joining in.

qa.q: How could a teacher help the class after the rainy break?
qa.a: Sister Agnes could ask each child what they personally said and invite them to make it right with Wasim, rather than accept “all of us”.

qa.q: If you were Wasim, what would you want from Hemant?
qa.a: An honest sorry and a turn to bowl; hearing “all of us” makes Wasim feel the whole class is against him.

grounding: The passage shows a child joining in excluding a classmate during a cramped rainy break and hiding behind “all of us said it”.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: It was the week before Diwali, and Class 5 was making a giant rangoli in the school corridor. When Trisha came to join, Meher said, "No space," and everyone turned their backs. Salma turned hers too. Trisha stood there holding her box of colours, then went and sat on the stairs. At home, Salma's mother asked about the rangoli. Salma mentioned Trisha. "Why didn't you let her join?" "Everyone was doing it, Ammi. Meher started it. I just did what the others did." Ammi put down the spoon. "If ten people turn their backs, how many backs does Trisha see?" Salma thought. "Ten." "And one of them is yours." Salma went quiet. The next morning she took an extra box of colours to school and walked straight to the stairs.

qa.q: Where did Trisha go after everyone turned their backs?
qa.a: She went and sat on the stairs.

qa.q: Why did Salma not feel fully responsible for leaving Trisha out?
qa.a: Because everyone was doing it and Meher started it, Salma felt the blame was shared, so her own part felt small and less guilty.

qa.q: What did Ammi say that helped Salma see her part?
qa.a: Ammi asked how many backs Trisha saw, showing that one of the ten was Salma's own.

qa.q: What was it like for Trisha to sit on the stairs holding her colours?
qa.a: Trisha probably felt rejected and lonely, shut out of the rangoli everyone else was making.

grounding: Before Diwali a girl joins classmates in shutting out another child and says everyone was doing it, until her mother points to her own share.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
"Mohit, why did Baljeet go home crying from the Christmas party?"
"I don't know, Papa."
"His mother called. She said the boys wouldn't let him play football."
"It wasn't me. Everybody said no."
"Did you say no?"
"...Everyone did. Arjit said he's too slow, and then everyone said it."
"And you?"
"I just said it because they did."
"So you said it."
"But it wasn't only me! There were eight of us."
"If it wasn't only you, then whose share was yours?"
Mohit kicked the table leg. "One eighth."
"Is one eighth zero?"
"No."
"What do you think Baljeet heard? One eighth of a no?"
"He heard eight no's."
Papa waited.
"Can I call him?" Mohit asked quietly. "And ask him to play tomorrow?"
"I think that's a good idea."

qa.q: Who said Baljeet was too slow?
qa.a: Arjit said he's too slow.

qa.q: Why did Mohit keep saying it wasn't only him?
qa.a: Mohit felt guilty but spread the blame across eight boys, so his own share felt too small to count.

qa.q: How did Papa help Mohit see his part without shaming him?
qa.a: Papa asked what share was Mohit's and whether one eighth was zero, letting Mohit work out his responsibility himself.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have felt hearing eight boys say no?
qa.a: Baljeet likely felt rejected and humiliated, enough to go home crying from the party.

grounding: At a Christmas party a boy joins seven others in refusing to let a classmate play and says everyone did it, until his father asks what his share was.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
The Holi I was ten, our building's gang of kids decided Chandrika from the fourth floor couldn't play with us. I don't even remember why. Someone said she cried too much. So when she came down with her pichkari, we all ran to the other side of the compound. I ran too.
When Ammi asked why Chandrika was sitting alone on the steps, covered in no colour at all, I said, "It wasn't me. Everyone decided." I really believed that made it okay. There were twelve of us, so it felt like my part was tiny, almost nothing.
Chandrika moved away the next year. I never said sorry. Now, whenever I'm in a group doing something unkind, I think of her on those steps. Twelve people did it. But I was one whole person of the twelve, not a twelfth of a person.
— Irfan

qa.q: How many kids ran to the other side of the compound?
qa.a: There were twelve of them.

qa.q: Why did Irfan feel it was okay to join in?
qa.a: With twelve kids doing it, Irfan felt the responsibility was shared out until Irfan's own part seemed tiny, so there was little guilt.

qa.q: What lesson did Irfan take into later group situations?
qa.a: That being one of many still means being one whole person who chose to act, so Irfan now stops to think before joining in.

qa.q: What was that Holi like for Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika sat alone on the steps with no colour, probably feeling rejected and hurt on a festival day.

grounding: An adult looks back on joining a group excluding a girl at Holi and saying everyone decided, when many shared the act.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Garba practice week, Class 4: note for the class file.
At lunch five girls sat on the steps and kept the space closed off with their bags. Parveen came with her tiffin, and Rashmi said, "This place is taken," and moved her bag over the last gap. Parveen ate alone near the water cooler, turning her roti over.
I spoke to Rashmi after lunch. She said, "But everyone was doing it, not only me. Mahi put her bag first." When I asked what Rashmi herself had done, she looked at her shoes. "I moved my bag."
What I did: sat with Parveen for the rest of lunch; phoned Rashmi's mother this evening; tomorrow I am pairing the girls for the garba circle so each one looks after one partner.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do when Parveen came with her tiffin?
qa.a: Rashmi said, "This place is taken," and moved her bag over the last gap.

qa.q: Why did "everyone was doing it" feel like a real excuse to Rashmi?
qa.a: With five girls blocking the steps, Rashmi felt like only a small part of it and so less guilty; when asked about her own action she looked at her shoes, embarrassed.

qa.q: What makes the teacher's next steps useful?
qa.a: The teacher comforted Parveen, phoned Rashmi's mother that evening, and plans to give each girl one partner, so no one can hide inside the group.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Parveen?
qa.a: Parveen ate alone by the water cooler turning her roti over, so she probably felt left out and hurt, however many girls shared the blame.

grounding: A child who joined in shutting out a classmate says everyone else was doing it, and a teacher turns the question to her own action.
